title: The Guarantee Stack: The Personal Exposure That Grows With Every Finance Facility You Sign
linkedin:
Most business owners can tell you the balance on every loan to the dollar.

Far fewer can tell you, without checking, the total amount they've personally guaranteed to repay if the business couldn't.

Here's the part that catches people out. Many guarantees aren't limited to the single facility they were signed alongside. An "all monies" or continuing guarantee covers future lending with that same institution too, including facilities opened years later with a different manager and no fresh conversation about what's actually at stake.

Paying off the original loan doesn't automatically release the guarantee behind it. Only a written release from the lender does that.

The pattern we see across owner-led businesses is that the full personal exposure gets calculated once, properly, and it's almost always a lender, an investor or a family solicitor who asks for it first. Usually mid capital raise or mid sale, when timelines are already tight and nobody wants a surprise.

The fix isn't complicated. List every facility, the guarantee attached to it, whether it's capped or open ended, and whether it covers one facility or all lending with that lender. Most owners who do this for the first time find at least one guarantee they assumed was closed out years ago.

Worth doing before the next facility gets added, not after.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

A lot of Queensland, New South Wales and Victorian business owners carry a personal guarantee on at least one business loan, overdraft or equipment finance facility, and most have never sat down to work out exactly what they have signed up for across every facility combined.

Here is what often gets missed. Many guarantees are not limited to the single loan they were signed alongside. If it is worded as a continuing or all monies guarantee, it can keep covering new lending with that same bank for years afterwards, even after the original loan has been fully repaid, unless the lender has given a formal written release.

This tends to surface at exactly the wrong moment, when a business is raising capital, taking on an investor, or going through a sale, and a lender or solicitor asks for a full picture that nobody has put together before.

The fix is straightforward. List every current facility, check the guarantee attached to each one, and confirm whether it is capped at a specific amount or open ended. Most business owners who do this for the first time find at least one surprise.
